title: Consensus (computer science)
summary: Consensus in distributed computing addresses how processes agree on a single data value despite failures. Processes propose candidate values and communicate to reach agreement. Protocols must handle faulty processes that may send conflicting data or stop entirely. The problem requires satisfying three core properties: termination, integrity, and agreement. Variants exist for crash versus Byzantine failures, and for synchronous versus asynchronous systems. In asynchronous settings, deterministic consensus is impossible with even one crash failure (FLP impossibility), though randomized algorithms can circumvent this. Consensus protocols are categorized as permissioned, assuming a fixed authenticated group, or permissionless, using artificial barriers like proof-of-work to prevent Sybil attacks.

mechanisms.title: Authenticated communication channels
mechanisms.explanation: Processes communicate through channels where message sources are known. Stronger 'written communication' models use digital signatures so receivers learn the full communication history, allowing protocols to tolerate more faults than 'oral communication' models where only the immediate source is known.

mechanisms.title: Fault tolerance properties
mechanisms.explanation: Consensus protocols must satisfy termination (every correct process eventually decides), integrity (if all correct processes propose the same value, that value must be decided), and agreement (all correct processes decide the same value). Protocols tolerating Byzantine failures additionally require that any decided value was proposed by a correct process.
